[RFCS.6.7] **A `FactAssert` records an assert ARRIVING, not a fact entering working
memory.** The two differ on a **no-op reassertion** — an assert whose identity
and every slot compare equal to a fact already live ([RARC.5.2.3]) — and the
atom must be written anyway.

The no-op discipline is a **working-memory** discipline, not a recording one.
Suppressing the WM change is load-bearing: series absorb and refraction depend
on a same-value re-assert being silent *to the network*. None of that reaches
the recorder, and [RARC.5.8.10] already puts the input hook at step (1) of the
consumption loop — **on arrival, before evaluation** — precisely so that what an
input did downstream cannot decide whether it was recorded.

**Why it cannot be dropped.** A no-op reassertion is an input the host supplied
and pumped for. Omit it and the recording holds neither the assert nor its pump,
so a replayer pumps fewer times than the original did. The trace is then a
complete-looking record of a run that did not happen: the `PumpBoundary`
([RFCS.22]) for that pump is there and the input that provoked it is not, so
the replay drives a pump against a working memory the recording never had.

**Replay is unaffected by the atom's presence.** A replayer injects the
recorded assert, the engine performs the identical no-op suppression, and the
same series-absorb and refraction outcomes follow. The atom restores the *input*
without disturbing the discipline.

⚠ **The volume cost is real and belongs to the input, not to this clause.** A
source re-reporting an unchanged value writes one `FactAssert` per report, each
report a suppressing recorder would drop included. That is the price [LFST.12.5] already named — *"the cost
of full fidelity"* — and an encoder must not reintroduce suppression as a
compression: [LFST.12.8] forbids sampling within a kind.

**The arriving assert precedes everything its evaluation produces.** An
**identity update** (`replaced` — same identity, a changed slot) records the
`FactAssert` first and then a `FactWithdraw` for the superseded fact with cause
`SUPERSEDED` ([RFCS.7a.2]), never a modify-in-place. A replayer that delivers
the assert re-derives the withdrawal after it, and compares it ([RFCS.7a.3]).

**A host retract is an input, and is ordered the same way.** The engine records
the `FactRetract` on arrival ([RARC.5.8.10]), before everything its evaluation
produces: the faults it raises and the withdrawals it cascades into follow it. A
replayer that delivers the retract re-derives them after it.

**An assert the engine refuses is recorded too.** A bounds refusal ([LERR.1.5])
of a host assert answers an input that arrived, so the engine records its
`FactAssert` and then the `BoundsError` its evaluation produced. A replayer
delivers the assert, the engine refuses it again, and the replay compares the
re-derived `BoundsError` with the recorded one. The engine's refusal of a
delivered input is not a replay failure. A host call refused because it is not
a well-formed input, such as an unknown schema or a slot value of the wrong kind
(RARC.5.2.6), records nothing and produces nothing.

**So does a host assert whose deadline would fall outside the `Time` range.**
A fact's TTL deadline is its entry stamp ([LTIM.2.8.6]) plus its TTL. Where
that sum would fall outside the representable range, the engine **must** refuse
the assert with `DS_ERR_TIME_RANGE` ([LTIM.1.1.5]) and leave the engine as it
was before the call: neither clock moves, no sample is recorded, nothing enters
working memory, and a pending `initial` block stays pending ([LGRA.24.3]). The
call is not a step ([LTIM.2.8.4]), though the deadline it is refused for is
reckoned from the sample that step would have taken. So a recording holds no
trace of it, and a replay has nothing to re-derive.

**A refusal inside a pump ends the firing, not the pump.** A bounds refusal
([LERR.1.5]) of a rule's action is recorded as a `BoundsError` in the firing
that attempted it. The firing stops at the refused action, by the prefix rule
of [LNUL.11.1]: the actions before it stand, and the actions after it do not
run. The pump goes on, and returns `DS_ERR_CONTRACT_BREACH`. A replayer treats that status from a replayed pump as
an outcome, not a failure: it continues past the pump, and compares the
re-derived `BoundsError` with the recorded one when that atom arrives. A
refusal the recording holds and the replay does not re-derive, or the reverse,
is a divergence.

**A halt is the other outcome a replayed input reports.** An input during which
the engine raises an `EngineError` returns `DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED` ([NCBK.2.9]):
a pump whose firing faults, an assert or retract whose propagation does. Where
the engine was running when the replayer delivered that input, the status is
the recorded run's halt, re-derived, and a replayer **must** treat it as an
outcome: it continues, and compares the re-derived `EngineError` with the
recorded one when that atom arrives. The `EngineError` is the tier's last
record ([LERR.1.4.7]), so this is how the replay of a halted run reaches the
end of its recording, which is filed as that run's evidence ([NDET.2.1]). An
`EngineError` the recording holds and the replay does not re-derive, or the
reverse, is a divergence.

**So is a status the pump's own evaluation reports.** A refused call
leaves `DS_ERR_NAN_REJECTED` as a pump's status ([NCBK.6.8]), and a read no
backing can answer leaves `DS_ERR_SERIES_NO_BACKING` ([NERR.6]). Each is a
one-shot report: the recorded run went on, and the recording holds what followed.
A replayer **must** treat either as an outcome and continue. No atom records
either, and the compare of what the firing did is what decides: a call the
recording holds and the replay refuses, or the reverse, is a divergence at that
`CallIssued`. A pump refused before its step ([NLFC.9.5]) leaves no `PumpBoundary`,
so a replay never delivers it.

Any other failing status from a replayed pump ends the replay, and so does the
refusal of an input that met an engine already halted: that input did not
reproduce the run.

**A replay's own status says whether it reproduced the run, not whether the run
halted.** A replay that reaches the end of its recording with every
compare clean **must** return `DS_OK`, and it returns `DS_OK` for a run that
halted too, having compared the `EngineError`. The halt latch says the run halted
([NCBK.2.11]), and a host that replays a recording reads both. So
`DS_ERR_ENGINE_HALTED` from a replay means one thing: the replay did not reproduce
the run, or met an engine already halted.
